rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation. This should show whether peaks are unretained, spread across the gradient, or still elute in the final hold, guiding later narrowing of the phi window and adjustment of slope.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only way to improve CRF is to shorten the run. Keeping the same wide window and temperature while reducing tG tests how much we can compress retention time before any pair approaches the 1.5 resolution threshold.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so now the goal is to find the fastest method that still keeps every adjacent pair at R at least 1.5. A shorter gradient directly tests how much more speed is possible before resolution starts to fail.

Resolution margins are still very large at 8 minutes, and the last peak is well before 10 minutes, so we can push to an even faster gradient. This probes the minimum viable tG on the same broad window before the earliest pair becomes limiting.

The worst pair still has comfortable resolution at tG 6 minutes, so another step shorter should reveal whether we can cut runtime further while staying above the 1.5 threshold. The same window and temperature isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

At 4 minutes the limiting pair is only slightly above the 1.5 cutoff, so the natural next step is to test the minimum allowed gradient time. This will show whether 4 minutes is already at the edge or whether an even faster fully resolved method is possible.

The last peak at 4.20 minutes in the 4-minute full-range run corresponds to only about 0.85 organic at elution, so the current 0.95 endpoint is wider than needed. Narrowing the phi window while keeping tG at 4 minutes should make the gradient shallower and recover margin on the critical early pair without sacrificing speed.

An intermediate phi1 should keep all peaks inside the gradient while preserving enough shallowing to beat the full-range 4-minute method on robustness.

Narrowing the window to phi1 0.80 improved the critical pair at tG 4 versus phi1 0.95, so it is worth retesting the 2-minute gradient under this shallower slope. This directly checks whether the minimum-time method can be rescued into full resolution by window optimization.

The 2-minute run improved from R 0.82 to 0.98 when phi1 was reduced from 0.95 to 0.80, so the limiting pair is responsive to slope. Pushing phi1 one more step lower may bring that pair to full resolution while keeping the method at the minimum gradient time.

The critical pair keeps improving as phi1 is lowered at fixed tG 2, and the last peak is still very early, so there is room to continue narrowing the endpoint. This tests whether the minimum-time method can cross the R = 1.5 threshold before the final compound is pushed excessively late.

The limiting pair continues to respond favorably to a lower phi1, and t_last remains comfortably below 10 minutes. Another step down in phi1 is the clearest way to see whether a 2-minute gradient can still reach full adjacent-pair resolution.

The first pair is still improving monotonically as phi1 decreases, and there is still no time penalty, so one more step is justified. This should show whether the 2-minute gradient can approach or reach full credit before the last compound starts to become problematic.
